key_terms.meaning: The study of programs whose performance on a task improves with experience, usually data.
A measurable property of one example, such as a crop's rainfall in mm or a transaction's amount in rupees.
The list of feature values for one example, written x = (x₁, x₂, …, xₙ).
The correct answer for an example, written y; present in labelled data, absent in unlabelled data.
A candidate rule h that maps a feature vector to a prediction, h: x → y.
The set H of all hypotheses a learner is allowed to consider.
Learning from labelled examples (x, y) to predict y for new x.
Learning structure from unlabelled data, with no correct answer given.
Learning by acting and receiving a scalar reward, so feedback is delayed and partial.
A problem with the task T, performance measure P and experience E stated explicitly.
Data used to fit the model and separate data used only to measure performance.
Low error on training data but high error on new data, because the model memorised noise.
High error on both training and test data, because the model is too simple.
A rule giving the probability of each value (discrete) or each range (continuous) of a variable.
Inferring a boolean rule from positive and negative examples of that concept.
The set of all hypotheses in H consistent with every training example seen so far.
The assumptions a learner uses to pick one general rule out of the many that fit the data.
Correct performance on examples the learner has never seen.

takeaways: Machine learning replaces hand-written rules with rules fitted from data, and its success is measured on data it has not seen.
Feedback decides the learning type: labels give supervised learning, no labels give unsupervised learning, a reward signal gives reinforcement learning.
A learning problem is only well posed when the task, the performance measure and the experience are all named.
Most real failures come from the data, not the algorithm: too little data, noisy labels, or a test set that does not match deployment.
Linear algebra supplies the vector language for features and weights; probability supplies the language for uncertainty and noise.
Concept learning is search: Find-S keeps one most specific hypothesis, while candidate elimination keeps the whole version space.
A learner can only generalise because of inductive bias, so a bias-free learner cannot decide anything about unseen examples.
Strong bias learns fast from little data but may be wrong; weak bias needs more data but can fit finer patterns.
bank_note: Long answers here are judged on definitions with a worked example, a traced algorithm (Find-S or candidate elimination), and a clear statement of inductive bias, not on listing many algorithms.

bank.q: Define machine learning in the form of a program that improves with experience. Explain five application areas and state, for each, what is the input and what is the output.
outline: Definition in terms of task T, performance P, experience E
Spam filtering: email text features in, spam or not-spam out
Medical screening: test values in, risk label out
Crop yield prediction: soil, rainfall, area in, yield in kg per hectare out
Recommendation and fraud detection as further examples
Why performance must be measured on unseen data

bank.q: Explain supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning. For each, state the feedback available and give two applications.
outline: Supervised: labelled pairs (x, y), classification and regression examples
Unsupervised: no labels, clustering and dimensionality reduction examples
Reinforcement: reward signal, agent, state, action, delayed feedback
Comparison table of data, feedback and goal
One Indian context example such as UPI fraud detection or a recommendation feed

bank.q: What is a well-posed learning problem? Explain with the three components using a checkers-playing program as the example.
outline: Statement of task T, performance measure P, experience E
Checkers: T = play checkers, P = percent of games won against opponents, E = games played against itself
Contrast with a badly stated goal such as 'learn checkers'
Why the performance measure must be fixed before training
Effect of choosing a different P on the learned behaviour

bank.q: Explain concept learning as a search problem. Define general-to-specific ordering of hypotheses and show how it organises the hypothesis space.
outline: Definition of concept, positive and negative examples
Hypothesis as a conjunction of attribute constraints
More-general-than-or-equal relation and why it is a partial order
Hypothesis space as a lattice with the most general and most specific hypotheses
Search without backtracking from general to specific or the reverse
Limitation: the space may be large or the target concept may not be expressible

bank.q: Describe the inductive bias of Find-S, of candidate elimination, and of a decision-tree learner that prefers shorter trees.
outline: Meaning of inductive bias
Find-S: bias is the choice of the most specific hypothesis consistent with the data
Candidate elimination: bias is the hypothesis space itself plus the consistency requirement
Decision tree: preference bias for shorter trees over longer ones
Difference between a restriction bias and a preference bias
Why a learner with no bias cannot generalise

bank.q: A dataset has attributes Sky (Sunny, Rainy), Temperature (Warm, Cold) and Humidity (Normal, High), and the concept is PlayTennis. Trace the Find-S algorithm on a given sequence of examples and state the final hypothesis.
outline: Initialise h to the most specific hypothesis, all attributes at their null value
Read each example in order
Update only on positive examples: replace a null with the example's value, or generalise to '?' on mismatch
Ignore negative examples unless they contradict h, which signals noise
Write the final hypothesis as a conjunction of attribute constraints
State the weakness: the result depends on example order and on the first positive example

bank.q: Apply the candidate elimination algorithm to the same PlayTennis data. Show the general boundary G and specific boundary S after each example and hence the version space.
outline: Initialise S to the most specific hypothesis and G to the most general hypothesis {?, ?, ?}
Positive example: generalise S, remove from G any hypothesis that does not cover it
Negative example: specialise G so that it excludes the example, keep S unchanged
Correct treatment of a hypothesis in G that is more specific than a hypothesis in S
Final version space described as everything between S and G
Note that the version space shrinks monotonically and can become empty with noise

bank.q: Design a learning system for predicting whether a farmer's crop will fail, covering task, performance measure, experience, features, data split and evaluation.
outline: Task statement and decision the output supports
Performance measure such as recall on the failure class, not accuracy alone
Experience: which fields, which seasons, how many labelled records
Feature list with units and how each would be collected
Train, validation and test split; keeping the same season out of both sides
Baseline to beat and error analysis loop
Deployment and monitoring concerns such as domain shift

bank.q: Compute the mean, variance and correlation between two features, then standardise both features. Explain in one paragraph why standardisation matters before a distance-based method such as k-nearest neighbours.
outline: Correct formulas with units and n or n−1 in the denominator
Correlation as covariance divided by the product of standard deviations, between −1 and +1
Standardisation z = (x − mean) / standard deviation
Distance dominated by the feature with the larger scale without it
Worked numeric substitution
Interpretation of a positive and a negative correlation

bank.q: Discuss the main challenges in machine learning under the headings data, model and evaluation. Give one concrete failure for each heading.
outline: Data: insufficient quantity, noisy labels, missing values, class imbalance, biased sampling
Model: overfitting, underfitting, curse of dimensionality, poor inductive bias for the problem
Evaluation: leakage between train and test, wrong metric, distribution shift at deployment
Each failure tied to a realistic example
Mitigations: more and cleaner data, regularisation, cross-validation, held-out testing

bank.q: Explain the bias-variance trade-off. Relate it to model complexity, training error, test error and the size of the training set.
outline: Expected squared error split into bias², variance and irreducible noise
High bias: simple model, underfits, both errors high
High variance: complex model, small training error, large test error
Effect of increasing training data on variance
Regularisation as a way to trade variance for bias
How cross-validation estimates test error and guides the choice

bank.q: A hospital wants a screening tool for a disease that affects 1 in 1000 people. Compare accuracy with precision, recall and the confusion matrix as the reported metric, and recommend a design.
outline: Confusion matrix layout: true positive, false positive, false negative, true negative
Why accuracy is misleading when the classes are imbalanced: a model that always says 'no' scores 99.9 percent
Recall as the fraction of true cases found; the cost of a false negative in screening
Precision and the cost of false positives such as extra tests and anxiety
Recommended metric and decision threshold chosen from the cost of each error
Need for calibration and for testing on a sample with the real prevalence

bank.q: Compare Find-S, candidate elimination and a decision-tree learner on the same concept-learning task. Which would you choose and why?
outline: What each returns: one hypothesis, the whole version space, a tree
Sensitivity to example order and to noise
Handling of negative examples only through consistency
Expressiveness: conjunctions only versus disjunctions through trees
Cost: number of hypotheses examined
Decision justified by what the user needs, a single rule or a ranked set of rules

bank.q: Trace the full path from a business question to a deployed model: problem framing, data preparation, model choice, evaluation and monitoring. Use a UPI fraud detection example.
outline: Framing as a well-posed problem with task, performance measure and experience
Label definition: which transactions count as fraud, and the delay in confirming them
Feature engineering from transaction amount, time, device and merchant history
Imbalance and the choice of precision, recall or cost-weighted metric
Model choice and a held-out or time-based split
Threshold selection and the human review queue
Monitoring for domain shift: new fraud patterns change the input distribution

glossary.def: A change in behaviour or performance that comes from experience rather than from explicit programming.
The exact job the learned program must do, such as classify or predict a number.
The number used to judge the program on the task, for example accuracy or recall.
The data or interactions the program learns from.
A candidate rule that maps a feature vector to a prediction or label.
The set of all hypotheses the learner is allowed to search.
A hypothesis that gives the correct label for every training example seen so far.
The set of all hypotheses consistent with the training data.
The most general hypotheses in the version space.
The most specific hypotheses in the version space.
An example for which the target concept is true.
An example for which the target concept is false.
Learning a mapping from inputs to outputs using labelled example pairs.
Supervised learning where the label is one of a finite set of classes.
Supervised learning where the label is a real number with units.
Unsupervised grouping of examples so that similar examples fall in the same group.
A scalar signal in reinforcement learning telling the agent how good the last action was.
The set of assumptions that lets a learner rank or restrict hypotheses beyond the data.
The expected error of a learned model on new examples drawn from the same distribution.
Fitting noise in the training data so that performance on new data drops.
Adding a penalty on model size or weight magnitude to reduce overfitting.
An ordered list of numbers, used here to hold the feature values of one example.
A variable whose value is uncertain and is described by a probability distribution.
Summing or integrating a joint distribution over one variable to get the distribution of the others.
A change in the input distribution between training and deployment that lowers performance.
